claims.text: The baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy forms multiple crystalline phases under slow cooling.
The baseline alloy forms several primary non-eutectic phases.
The baseline alloy exhibits a multistep crystallization sequence.
Faster cooling reduces the number of crystalline phases in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Very rapid cooling by melt spinning produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 structure.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy promote amorphous-phase formation in the baseline alloy during extremely fast cooling.
Adding 2 at.% boron to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will increase chemical and structural heterogeneity.
Boron-induced heterogeneity will disrupt ordered clusters that act as nucleation sites.
Boron is a glass-forming metalloid in the relevant alloy context.
Boron interferes with atomic ordering among the transition metals in this alloy.
Boron breaks up the connectivity of metallic clusters.
Disruption of atomic-size and bonding order can impede crystal nucleation and grain growth and thereby favor amorphous structures.
Adding 2 at.% boron will increase the critical cooling rate required for primary crystallization.
Adding 2 at.% boron will increase the retained amorphous fraction relative to the baseline alloy.
Adding 2 at.% boron will improve thermal stability during reheating.
Adding 2 at.% boron will shift crystallization onset or peak temperatures to higher temperatures.
Adding 2 at.% boron will suppress the multistep crystallization sequence and reduce primary non-eutectic phase formation.
Enhanced glass formation requires a cooling rate above approximately 10^5 K/s.
A melt-spun ribbon thickness of approximately 20 µm provides the specified rapid-cooling regime.
Reheating at approximately 100 K/min only to about 0.9 times T_cryst is an appropriate boundary for monitoring crystallization onset.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says boron increases the critical cooling rate while claiming enhanced glass formation. Under the conventional definition—the minimum cooling rate needed to avoid crystallization—an increased critical cooling rate indicates poorer, not better, glass-forming ability. The text may instead mean that crystallization remains suppressed to slower cooling, but it does not define the term that way.

The reheating boundary stops at about 0.9×T_cryst, whereas the falsification experiment requires measuring crystallization onset and peak profiles. If T_cryst denotes the onset or peak temperature, stopping below it cannot directly measure the required onset or complete peak.
